newsitem.title: USA: Dollar ends broadly lower as Treasuries slump.
newsitem.headline: Dollar ends broadly lower as Treasuries slump.

text.p: The dollar ended lower against the mark and the yen on Thursday, hurt by a sharp decline in the U.S. Treasury bond market.

Treasuries were hit by a combination of jitters ahead of Friday's November jobs report, profit-taking and technical factors. Traders said much of the selling came from foreign investors and helped push the dollar lower against other major currencies.

"The dollar traded almost in lockstep with the bonds and the bonds got killed," said Alfonso Alejo, senior trader at Sakura Bank Ltd. The benchmark 30-year bond lost 47/32, or $14.6875 per $1,000 face value, and its yield, which moves in the opposite direction, climbed to 6.51 percent from Wednesday's 6.40 percent.
The greenback ended the session at 1.5512 marks, down from 1.5605 at Wednesday's close. Against the yen, the dollar retreated as well, falling to 112.33 yen from 113.15.

Contributing to the dollar's weakness against the yen was a rumour circulating overnight that influential Japanese Ministry of Finance official Eisuke Sakakibara would call for a range of 108 to 110 in the dollar/yen rate in a television interview.

Although Sakakibara, known as "Mr. Yen" for the impact his comments have had on the currency in the past, failed to confirm the rumour when he spoke on Japanese television later in the day, the dollar was unable to recover against the yen.

The dollar's downward drift against the mark followed German data overnight that showed an increase in unemployment to a record high 10.7 percent in November. Despite the weak data, and other recent signs of economic sluggishness in Germany, the Bundesbank did not cut interest rates at its council meeting on Thursday.
Although steady policy had been widely expected, the central bank's decision did give the mark modest support, traders said.
In other trading, the pound stumbled, mainly against the mark and yen, after Bank of England Governor Eddie George downplayed the urgency for a British rate rise.

Because higher interest rates tend to make a country's assets, including its currency, more attractive, expectations of a rate increase had helped push sterling to four-year peaks of 2.6370 marks and $1.6905 in recent weeks.
While noting that a rate increase was needed, George said there was "no urgent need for a dramatic step." His remark knocked sterling to overnight session lows of 2.5155 marks and $1.6095.
Sterling recovered during U.S. trading hours to end the session at $1.6345, down from $1.6433 on Wednesday. But analysts said the pound remains vulnerable.
The dollar fell to 1.3135 Swiss francs from 1.3210 on Wednesday. It rose modestly to Canadian $1.3565 from C$1.3538.
